title: Businesses have responsibility to stop modern slavery. So do police
author: Marika McAdam
text: |Human rights, explained.Australia has a chance to lift its modern slavery regime to meet international standards with proposals to establish a criminal offence of “failing to prevent” modern slavery in its operations and supply chain (Aleksi Partanen/Unsplash)Businesses have responsibility to stop modern slavery. So do policeA criminal offence for modern slavery is now on the table – but laws alone cannot replace proactive policing.Marika McAdam20 November 20264 min read|Businesses have responsibility to stop modern slavery. So do policeBusinesses have responsibility to stop modern slavery. So do police“Modern slavery” has long been framed as a human rights violation. The extent to which it also constitutes crime is harder to talk about.Regulatory regimes governing responsible business conduct are leaning towards mandatory human rights due diligence efforts to require action and accountability beyond mere reporting.The United Kingdom has recently announced (Opens in new window) that it will legislate for big businesses to not only report human rights and labour exploitation risks within their operations and supply chains, but also to address those risks. This effort to align with international standards in the OECD Guidelines for Responsible Business Conduct (Opens in new window) and the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (Opens in new window) is one that Australia’s Anti-Slavery Commissioner Chris Evans has also welcomed (Opens in new window).Australia has a chance to lift its modern slavery regime to meet international standards with proposals to establish a criminal offence of “failing to prevent” modern slavery in its operations and supply chain. The framework the Anti-Slavery Commissioner proposed (Opens in new window) in October advocates a “carefully designed criminal offence” that applies to the most serious criminal conduct, as a component of a broader framework response alongside a due diligence obligation. In a recent report (Opens in new window), New South Wales Anti-Slavery Commissioner James Cockayne alleged links between labour hire practices and organised criminal groups involved in the trade of illicit tobacco and trafficking humans for the purpose of sexual exploitation. The findings follow the NSW government’s response (Opens in new window) to 31 recommendations made by the Modern Slavery Committee on the risks faced by temporary migrant workers in regional NSW, which makes no reference to organised crime. Cockayne points to “the lack of effective, proactive policing” as a central deficiency of Australia’s response to modern slavery.Proactive, intelligence-led policing against modern slavery – which includes human trafficking and other crimes – is the only approach that can meaningfully disrupt criminal operations. Responding to isolated incidents of human exploitation cannot identify linkages between different forms of organised crime occurring globally in which criminals do not participate in one crime type but several (Opens in new window).The shortcomings of reactive policing have become painfully apparent in recent manifestations of slavery. Hundreds of thousands of people have been trafficked (Opens in new window) into the global cyber-scam industry in Southeast Asia and beyond (Opens in new window), forced – sometimes even tortured (Opens in new window) – to commit crime. Some companies implicated may be ignorant of the exploitation occurring in their supply chains, but others have been established for that purpose, providing financial and logistic support to a trillion-dollar scam economy (Opens in new window) alongside licit activities. As police scramble to keep up, the “whack-a-mole” metaphor has become hackneyed – making the point that only proactive efforts can hope to get ahead of the diffusion of criminality.The UN reports (Opens in new window) that trafficking in persons is no longer limited to traditional forms, but that digital technologies have transformed methods of recruitment, control and exploitation. To situate modern slavery in this context, supply chains no longer comprise raw materials, manufacturers, distributors, retailers and consumers, but also social media platforms, crypto-companies, AdTech, artificial intelligence (AI) and other emerging technology companies whose business models are opaque by design (Opens in new window).Confronting the human rights abuses and the serious, organised crimes that occur along those chains is not the work of a regulatory regime in a country, but of several regimes across several countries, ideally working in tandem.The art of achieving a comprehensive response is to bring legal regimes together to disrupt criminals without discouraging businesses from innovative and pragmatic efforts against exploitation.The call to respond to the link between modern slavery and organised crime is not revolutionary. It isn’t even new. The origin of global understanding of trafficking in persons was achieved within the framework of a treaty (Opens in new window) on transnational organised crime. To the extent that modern slavery intersects with human trafficking (a relationship long debated (Opens in new window) by practitioners and scholars), criminal dimensions must also be addressed by a legal regime agile enough to respond.As others have argued (Opens in new window), neither criminal law, nor the regulation of business supply chains, can provide a complete response to “modern slavery”, a phenomenon that has proven both conceptually and practically amorphous. The authors of the newly published book Transforming Business (Opens in new window) highlight that human rights responsibilities must be supported by governments establishing the enabling environment that incentivises businesses to fulfil their human rights responsibilities. So too must countries take a proactive policing approach to businesses that are not on a good faith human rights journey but are pursuing a criminal agenda.On 7 August 1865, a former slave, Jourdon Anderson, wrote a letter (Opens in new window) to his former enslaver. The latter had requested Jourdon and his wife Mandy return to his service. Jourdon, in setting out his conditions (including payment for years of unpaid wages, with interest) as a test of the sincerity of the invitation, reminded his former master of violence he perpetrated or did not prevent, and reflected that “surely there will be a day of reckoning for those who defraud the labourer of his hire”.In reckoning with the modern slavery of today, businesses must not only be held to account for their human rights failures, but also for their criminal actions. The art of achieving a comprehensive response is to bring legal regimes together (Opens in new window) to disrupt criminals without discouraging businesses from innovative and pragmatic efforts against exploitation.About the authorMarika McAdamDr Marika McAdam is an independent adviser on criminal justice and human rights.TopicsHuman rightsTransnational crimeInternational lawAustraliaThe Interpreter on Human rightsExplore The InterpreterIndiaCockroach Janata Party: how India tried to delete its protesters’ app18 November 2026AnuragAfricaAustralia talks tough on Sudan but won’t confront patrons in UAE11 November 2026Daniela GavshonAustraliaAustralia has picked its national soundtrack – but not its story11 November 2026Stacy JarvisMore on Human rightsExplore Human rightsResearchUse of political violence: Political actors inflame communal violence in IndiaAnalysis by Lydia Khalil, Peter Woodrow + 2 othersReportDemocratic Erosion ReportReport by Lydia Khalil, Peter Woodrow + 2 othersResearchAfter annexation: How China plans to run TaiwanAnalysis by Richard McGregor, Jude BlanchetteEvent ReplayBook launch | Gough Whitlam: The Vista of the New by Troy Bramston Troy Bramston, David Dutton
